mn12:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the grove outside the city to the west.
mn12:2.1: Now on that occasion Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis had recently forsaken this Dhamma and Discipline.
mn12:2.2: He was making this statement before the Vesālī Assembly:
mn12:2.3: ‘The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state (dhamma).
mn12:2.4: The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by human thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him,
mn12:2.5: and whoever is taught that Dhamma for his benefit, it (only) leads rightly to the exhaustion of suffering in him when he practises it, (but not to anything else).’
mn12:3.1: Then, it being morning, the venerable Sāriputta dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe he went into Vesālī for alms.
mn12:3.2: Then he heard of (what) Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis, was saying.
mn12:3.6: When he had wandered for alms in Vesālī and had returned from his alms-round, after his meal, he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he told the Blessed One what had taken place.
mn12:4.1: ‘Sāriputta, the misguided man Sunakkhatta is angry,
mn12:4.2: and his words are spoken out of anger.
mn12:4.3: Thinking to condemn the Tathāgata, he actually commends the Tathāgata;
mn12:4.4: for it is a commendation of the Tathāgata to say of him
mn12:4.5: “and whoever is taught the Dhamma for his benefit, it (only) leads rightly to the exhaustion of suffering in him who practises it (but not to anything else)”.’
mn12:5.1: ‘Sāriputta, this misguided man Sunakkhatta will never infer of me according to Dhamma that:
mn12:5.2: “That Blessed One is such since he is Arahant, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, Enlightened, Blessed.”
mn12:6.1: ‘And he will never infer of me according to Dhamma:
mn12:6.2: “That Blessed One is such that he enjoys the various kinds of (supernormal) success; having been one he becomes many, having been many he becomes one: he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain, as through space; he dives in and out of earth as though it were water; he goes on unbroken water as though it were earth; seated cross-legged he travels in space like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun so mighty and powerful; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the world of Divinity (Brahmā).”
mn12:7.1: ‘And he will never infer of me according to Dhamma:
mn12:7.2: “That Blessed One is such that with the heavenly ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, the heavenly and the human, those that are far as well as near.”
mn12:8.1: ‘And he will never infer of me according to Dhamma:
mn12:8.2: “That Blessed One is such that he encompasses with his mind the minds of other beings, other persons.
mn12:8.3: He understands the mind affected by lust as affected by lust
mn12:8.4: and the mind unaffected by lust as unaffected by lust;
mn12:8.5: he understands the mind affected by hate as affected by hate
mn12:8.6: and the mind unaffected by hate as unaffected by hate;
mn12:8.7: he understands the mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion
mn12:8.8: and the mind unaffected by delusion as unaffected by delusion;
mn12:8.9: he understands the contracted mind as contracted
mn12:8.10: and the distracted mind as distracted;
mn12:8.11: he understands the exalted mind as exalted
mn12:8.12: and the unexalted mind as unexalted;
mn12:8.13: he understands the surpassed mind as surpassed
mn12:8.14: and the unsurpassed mind as unsurpassed;
mn12:8.15: he understands the concentrated mind as concentrated
mn12:8.16: and the unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated;
mn12:8.17: he understands the liberated mind as liberated
mn12:8.18: and the unliberated mind as unliberated.”
mn12:9.1: ‘Sāriputta, a Tathāgata has these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which he claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar before the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.
mn12:10.1: (1) ‘Here a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
mn12:10.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power that a Tathāgata has by virtue of which he claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar before the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.
mn12:11.1: (2) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the ripening of kammas undertaken, past, future and present, with possiblities and with causes.
mn12:11.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:12.1: (3) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, whither all ways lead.
mn12:12.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:13.1: (4) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the world with its many and differing elements.
mn12:13.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:14.1: (5) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is how beings have different inclinations.
mn12:14.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:15.1: (6) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the disposition of the faculties of other beings, other persons.
mn12:15.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:16.1: (7) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the defilement of, the cleansing of and the emergence from the jhānas, liberations, concentrations and attainments.
mn12:16.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:17.1: (8) ‘Again, a Tathāgata recollects his manifold past life, that is to say, one birth, two births … five births, ten births … fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of (universal) contraction, many aeons of (universal) expansion, many aeons of (universal) contraction and expansion: There I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named... such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared here. Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.
mn12:17.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:18.1: (9) ‘Again, a Tathāgata, with the heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved: understands how beings pass on according to their kammas, thus: “These worthy beings who are ill-conducted in body, speech and mind, revilers of the Noble Ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their kammas, have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these worthy beings who are well-conducted in body, speech and mind, not revilers of the Noble Ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their kammas, have, on the dissolution of the body after death, appeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”, thus with heavenly eyesight … he sees beings passing away and reappearing … He understands how beings pass on according to their kammas.
mn12:18.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …
mn12:19.1: (10) ‘Again, a Tathāgata, by realization himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of the heart and deliverance by understanding that are taintless, with (final) exhaustion of taints.
mn12:19.2: And that is a Tathāgata’s power that a Tathāgata has, by virtue of which he claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.
mn12:20.1: ‘A Tathāgata has these ten Tathāgata’s Powers, possessing which he claims the herd-leader’s place …
mn12:21.1: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus, say:
mn12:21.2: “The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state.
mn12:21.3: The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him”,
mn12:21.4: then unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).
mn12:21.5: Just as a bhikkhu perfected in virtue, concentration and understanding would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it (will) happen in this case, I say, that
mn12:21.6: unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, then as (sure as if he had been) carried off (and) put (there) so he (will find himself) in hell.
mn12:22.1: ‘Sāriputta, there are four kinds of intrepidity, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.
mn12:23.1: ‘Here I can see no reason why any monk or divine or god or māra or divinity at all in the world could, in accordance with the Dhamma, accuse me thus: “While you claim discovery of full enlightenment, you are not enlightened in these dhammas.”
mn12:23.2: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity.
mn12:24.1: ‘I can see no reason why any monk … could … accuse me thus: “While you claim to have exhausted the taints, these taints are unexhausted in you.”
mn12:24.2: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in … intrepidity.
mn12:25.1: ‘I can see no reason why any monk … could … accuse me thus: “Those dhammas which are said by you to be obstructive are not in fact obstructive to one who practises them.”
mn12:25.2: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in … intrepidity.
mn12:26.1: ‘I can see no reason why any monk … could … accuse me thus: “Whoever is taught the Dhamma by you for his benefit, it does not lead rightly to the exhaustion of suffering in him when he practises it.”
mn12:26.2: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity.
mn12:27.1: ‘These are the four kinds of intrepidity possessing which a Tathāgata claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.
mn12:28.1: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus …
mn12:28.2: “The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state. The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him”,
mn12:28.3: then unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).
mn12:28.4: Just as a bhikkhu perfected in virtue, concentration and understanding would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it (will) happen in this case, I say,
mn12:28.5: that unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, then as (sure as if he had been) carried off (and) put (there) so he (will find himself) in hell.
mn12:29.3: A warrior-nobles’ assembly, a divines’ assembly, a householders’ assembly, a monks’ assembly, an assembly of gods of the Four Kings, an assembly of gods of the Thirty-three, a Māra’s assembly, a Divinities’ assembly.
mn12:29.5: Possessing these four kinds of intrepidity, a Tathāgata approaches and goes into these eight kinds of assembly.
mn12:29.6: ‘I have had direct knowledge, as a visitor, of many hundred warrior-noble caste assemblies.
mn12:29.7: And formerly, I had sat with them there and talked and held converse with them.
mn12:29.8: I see no reason why fear or timidity should come upon me there.
mn12:29.9: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity.
mn12:30.1: ‘I have had direct knowledge, as a visitor, of many hundred divine-caste assemblies ...
mn12:30.4: ‘... assemblies of gods of the Four Kings ...
mn12:30.5: ‘... assemblies of gods of the Thirty-Three ...
mn12:30.10: I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity. (These are the eight kinds of assemblies).
mn12:31.1: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus …
mn12:31.3: unless he abandons that assertion … carried off (and) put … in hell.
mn12:32.1: ‘Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of generation.
mn12:32.3: Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, spontaneous generation.
mn12:33.2: There are beings born by breaking out of the shell of an egg;
mn12:33.5: There are those beings born by breaking out from the caul;
mn12:33.8: There are those beings born in a rotten fish, in a rotten corpse, or in rotten dough, or in a cesspit or in a sewer;
mn12:33.11: There are gods and denizens of hell and certain human beings and certain denizens of the states of deprivation, of spontaneous generation;
mn12:33.13: ‘These are the four kinds of generation.
mn12:34.1: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus …
mn12:34.3: unless he abandons that assertion … carried off (and) put … in hell.
mn12:35.3: Hell, the animal womb, the realm of ghosts, human beings and gods.
mn12:36.1: (1) ‘I understand hell; and the path and the way leading to hell,
mn12:36.2: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell; that too I understand.
mn12:36.3: (2) ‘I understand the animal womb; and the path and the way leading to the animal womb,
mn12:36.4: where he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in the animal womb; that too I understand.
mn12:36.5: (3) ‘I understand the realm of ghosts; and the path and way leading to the realm of ghosts,
mn12:36.6: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in the realm of ghosts; that too I understand.
mn12:36.7: (4) ‘I understand human beings; and the path and the way leading to the human world,
mn12:36.8: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear among human beings; that too I understand.
mn12:36.9: (5) ‘I understand the gods; and the path and the way leading to the world of gods,
mn12:36.10: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world; that too I understand.
mn12:36.11: (6) ‘I understand Nibbāna; and the path and the way leading to Nibbāna,
mn12:36.12: whereon he who has entered will, by realization himself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and deliverance of understanding that are taint-free, with exhaustion of taints; that too I understand.
mn12:37.1: (1) ‘By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:
mn12:37.2: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell.”
mn12:37.3: And then later on with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell and is experiencing unremitting, painful, racking, piercing feelings.
mn12:37.4: ‘Suppose there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height full of glowing coals without flame or smoke;
mn12:37.5: and then a man, scorched and exhausted by the hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to the same charcoal pit;
mn12:37.6: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:
mn12:37.7: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same charcoal pit”;
mn12:37.8: and then later on he sees that he has fallen into that charcoal pit and is experiencing unremitting painful, racking, piercing feelings;
mn12:37.9: so too, by encompassing mind with mind ...
mn12:38.1: (2) ‘By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:
mn12:38.2: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the animal womb.”
mn12:38.3: And then later on, with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the animal womb and is experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings.
mn12:38.4: ‘Suppose there were a cesspit more than a man’s height deep, full of filth;
mn12:38.5: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same cesspit;
mn12:38.6: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:
mn12:38.7: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same cesspit”;
mn12:38.8: and then later on he sees that he has fallen into the cesspit and is experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings;
mn12:38.9: so too, by encompassing mind with mind …
mn12:39.1: (3) ‘By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:
mn12:39.2: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the realm of ghosts.
mn12:39.3: And then later on … I see that … he has reappeared in the realm of ghosts and is experiencing much painful feeling.
mn12:39.4: ‘Suppose there were a tree growing on uneven ground with scanty foliage casting a dappled shade;
mn12:39.5: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same tree;
mn12:39.6: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:
mn12:39.7: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same tree”;
mn12:39.8: and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in the shade of that tree experiencing much painful feeling;
mn12:39.9: so too by encompassing mind with mind …
mn12:40.1: By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear among human beings.”
mn12:40.3: And then later on … I see that … he has reappeared among human beings and is experiencing much pleasant feeling.
mn12:40.4: Suppose there were a tree growing on even ground with thick foliage casting a deep shade;
mn12:40.5: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same tree;

mn12:40.8: and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in the shade of that tree experiencing much pleasant feeling;
mn12:40.9: so too, encompassing mind with mind …
mn12:41.1: By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: “This person so behaves …
mn12:41.2: that … after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.”
mn12:41.3: And then later on … I see that … he has reappeared in a happy destination, in the heavenly world and is experiencing unremitting pleasant feelings.
mn12:41.4: Suppose there were a mansion, and in it an upper chamber plastered within and without, shut off, secured by bars, and with shuttered windows,
mn12:41.5: and in it a couch spread with rugs and blankets and sheets, with a deerskin coverlet, and with a canopy as well as crimson pillow for both (head and feet);
mn12:41.6: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same mansion;
mn12:41.7: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:
mn12:41.8: “This person so behaves … that he will come to this same mansion;
mn12:41.9: and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in that upper chamber in that mansion experiencing unremitting pleasant feelings,
mn12:41.10: so too, by encompassing mind with mind …
mn12:42.1: By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:
mn12:42.2: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such that, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the heart’s deliverance and deliverance by understanding that are taint-free, with exhaustion of taints.”
mn12:42.3: And then later on I see that by realization for himself with direct knowledge he here and now enters upon and abides in the heart’s deliverance and deliverance by understanding that are taint-free, with exhaustion of taints, and is experiencing unremitting pleasant feeling.
mn12:42.4: ‘Suppose there were a pond with clean, agreeable, cool water, transparent, with smooth banks and delightful,
mn12:42.6: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed towards that same pond;
mn12:42.7: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:43.1: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone, knowing and seeing me thus say:
mn12:43.2: “The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state.
mn12:43.3: The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him”,
mn12:43.4: then unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind, and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).
mn12:43.5: Just as a bhikkhu perfected in virtue, concentration and understanding would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it (will) happen in this case, I say,
mn12:43.6: that unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind, and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).
mn12:44.1: ‘Sāriputta, I have had direct knowledge of (what is called) the four-factored life divine as one who has lived it.
mn12:44.2: I have practised the extreme of asceticism, of coarseness, of scrupulousness, and of seclusion.
mn12:45.1: ‘Such was my asceticism here that I went naked, rejecting conventions, licking my hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; I did not accept a thing brought or a thing specially made or an invitation;
mn12:45.2: I received nothing from out of a pot, from out of a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a woman with child, from a woman giving suck, from (where) a woman was lying with a man, from where food was advertised to be distributed, from where a dog was waiting, from where flies were buzzing; I accepted no fish or meat, I drank no liquor, wine or besotting drink.
mn12:45.3: I kept to one house, to one morsel; I kept to two houses, to two morsels … I kept to seven houses, to seven morsels.
mn12:45.4: I lived on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls … on seven saucerfuls, a day;
mn12:45.5: I took food once a day, once each two days, … once each seven days; and so on, up to once each fortnight. I dwelt pursuing the practice of taking food at stated intervals.
mn12:45.6: I was an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or hide-parings, or moss, or ricebran, or rinsings, or sesamum flour, or grass, or cowdung. I lived on forest roots and on fruits as a feeder on windfalls.
mn12:45.7: I clothed myself in hemp, in hemp mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in kusa-grass fabric, in bark fabric, in wood (shavings) fabric, in head-hair wool, in animal wool, in owls’ wings.
mn12:45.8: I was one who pulled out hair and beard, pursuing the practice of pulling out hair and beard.
mn12:45.9: I was one who stood continuously, rejecting seats.
mn12:45.10: I was one who squatted continuously, devoted to maintaining the squatting position.
mn12:45.11: I was one who used a mattress of spikes; I made a mattress of spikes my bed.
mn12:45.12: I dwelt pursuing the practice of bathing in water for the third time by nightfall.
mn12:46.3: just as the bole of a plane tree, accumulating over the years, cakes and flakes off, so too, the dust and dirt, accumlating over the years, caked on my body and flaked off.
mn12:46.5: “Oh, let me rub this dust and dirt off with my hand, or let another rub this dust and dirt off with his hand”—
mn12:46.6: it never occurred to me thus.
mn12:47.2: I was always mindful in stepping forwards and stepping backwards: So much so that I was full of pity for even a drop of water, thus:
mn12:47.3: “Let me not hurt the tiny breathing things in the crevices of the ground”.
mn12:48.2: I would go away into some forest and dwell there.
mn12:48.3: And when I saw a cowherd or a shepherd or someone gathering grass or sticks, or a woodsman, I would flee from grove to grove, from thicket to thicket, from hollow to hollow, from hillock to hillock—
mn12:48.5: So that they should not see me or I see them.
mn12:48.6: Just as a forest-bred deer on seeing human beings flees from grove to grove, from thicket to thicket, from hollow to hollow, from hillock to hillock,
mn12:49.1: I would go on all fours to the byres when the cattle had gone out and the cowherds had left them, and I would feed on the young sucking-calves’ dung.
mn12:49.2: As long as my own excrement and urine lasted, I fed on my own excrement and urine.
mn12:49.3: Such was my great distortion in feeding.
mn12:50.1: I would go off to some awe-inspiring grove and dwell there—
mn12:50.3: normally it would make a man’s hair stand up if he were not free from lust.
mn12:50.4: I would dwell by night in the open and by day in the grove when those cold wintry nights came during the Eight-days Interval of Frost.
mn12:50.5: I would dwell by day in the open and by night in the grove in the last month of the hot season.
mn12:50.6: And there came to me spontaneously this stanza never heard before:
mn12:50.7: > Chilled by night and scorched by day,
mn12:50.9: > Naked, no fire to sit beside,
mn12:50.10: > The hermit yet pursues his quest.
mn12:51.1: ‘I would make my bed in a charnel ground with the bones of the dead for a pillow.
mn12:51.2: And cowherd boys came up and spat on me, made water on me, threw dirt at me, and poked sticks into my ears.
mn12:51.3: Yet I never knew the arising of an evil mind (thoughts) about them.
mn12:51.4: Such was my abiding in equanimity.
mn12:52.1: ‘Sāriputta, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:
mn12:52.5: and they eat kola-fruits, and they eat kola-fruit powder, and they drink kola-fruit water,
mn12:52.6: and they make many kinds of kola-fruit concoctions.
mn12:52.7: Now I have had direct knowledge of eating a single kola-fruit a day.
mn12:52.8: But, Sāriputta, you may think that
mn12:52.9: the kola-fruit was bigger at that time,
mn12:52.10: yet you should not regard it so:
mn12:52.11: the kola-fuit was then at most the same size as now.
mn12:52.12: Through feeding on a single kola-fruit a day, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.
mn12:52.13: Because of eating so little my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems.
mn12:52.14: Because of eating so little my backside became like a camel’s hoof.
mn12:52.15: Because of eating so little the projections on my spine stood out like corded beads.
mn12:52.16: Because of eating so little my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old roofless barn.
mn12:52.17: Because of eating so little the gleam of my eyes sunk far down in their sockets looked like the gleam of water sunk far down in a deep well.
mn12:52.18: Because of eating so little my scalp shrivelled and withered as a green gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun.
mn12:52.19: Because of eating so little, if I touched by belly skin, I encountered my backbone too; if I touched my backbone, I encountered my bell-skin too.
mn12:52.20: Because of eating so little, if I made water or evacuated my bowels, I fell over on my face there.
mn12:52.21: Because of eating so little, if I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body as I rubbed.
mn12:53-55.1: ‘There are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:
mn12:53-55.7: And they eat rice, and they eat rice powder, and they drink rice water,
mn12:53-55.8: and they make various kinds of rice concoctions.
mn12:53-55.9: Now I have had direct knowledge of eating a single rice grain a day.
mn12:53-55.10: But, Sāriputta, you may think that
mn12:53-55.11: the rice grain was bigger at that time;
mn12:53-55.12: yet you should not regard it so:
mn12:53-55.13: the rice grain was at most the same size as now.
mn12:53-55.14: Through feeding on a single rice grain a day my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.
mn12:53-55.23: the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body as I rubbed.’
mn12:56.1: ‘Yet, Sāriputta, by such deportment, by such practice, by such performance of difficult feats, I attained no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision higher than the human state (dhamma).
mn12:56.3: Because I did not attain this Noble Understanding, which, on being attained, being Noble and an outlet, rightly leads to the exhaustion of suffering in him who practise it.’
mn12:57.1: ‘Sāriputta, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:
mn12:57.2: “Purification comes about through (the process of) a round of rebirths (itself).”
mn12:57.3: But it is impossible to find the round of rebirths that I have not already gone the round of in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes:
mn12:57.4: and had I gone the round as a god in the Pure Abodes, I should never have returned to this world.
mn12:58.1: ‘There are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:
mn12:58.2: “Purification comes through (some particular kind of) rebirth.”
mn12:58.3: But it is impossible to find the kind of rebirth that I have not been reborn in already in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes: …
mn12:59.3: But it is impossible to find the kind of abode that I have not dwelt in … except for the Pure Abodes… .
mn12:60.3: But it is impossible to find the kind of sacrifice that has not already been offered up by me in this long journey, either as a head-anointed warrior-noble king or as a divine with great property.
mn12:61.3: But it is impossible to find the kind of fire that has not already been worshipped by me in this long journey, either as a head-anointed warrior-noble king or as a divine of great property.
mn12:62.1: ‘Sāriputta, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:
mn12:62.2: “As long as this good man is still young, a black-haired boy endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first phase of life, so long is he perfect in his lucid understanding.
mn12:62.3: But when this good man is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage, being eighty, ninety or a hundred years old, then the lucidity of his understanding is lost.”
mn12:62.4: But it should not be regarded so.
mn12:62.5: I am now old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage: my years have turned eighty.
mn12:62.6: Now suppose that I had four disciples with a hundred years’ life, a hundred years’ span, perfect in mindfulness, attentiveness, memory and lucidity of understanding—
mn12:62.7: just as a well-equipped archer, trained, practised and tested, could easily shoot a light arrow arrow across a palm’s shadow:
mn12:62.8: suppose they were even to that extent perfect in mindfulness, attentiveness, memory and lucidity of understanding—
mn12:62.9: and suppose that they continuously asked about the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and that I answered when asked and that they remembered each answer of mine and never asked a subsidiary question or paused except to eat, drink, chew, taste, make water, evacuate the bowels and rest in order to remove sleepiness and tiredness:
mn12:62.10: still the Tathāgata’s exposition of the Dhamma, his explanations of factors of the Dhamma, and his replies to questions, would be unexhausted.
mn12:62.11: But meanwhile those four disciples of mine with their hundred-years’ life, their hundred-years’ span, would have died at the end of those hundred years.
mn12:62.12: Sāriputta, even if you have to carry me about on a bed, still there will be no change in the lucidity of the Tathāgata’s understanding.
mn12:63.1: ‘Rightly speaking, were it to be said of someone.
mn12:63.2: “A being not subject to delusion has appeared in the world for the welfare and happiness of many, out of pity for the world, for the benefit, welfare and happiness of gods and men”, it is of me indeed that rightly speaking it should be said.’
mn12:64.1: Now on that occasion the venerable Nāgasamāla was standing behind the Blessed One fanning him.
mn12:64.2: Then he said to the Blessed One:
mn12:64.3: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous!
mn12:64.4: As I listened to this discourse the hairs of my body stood up.
mn12:64.5: Venerable sir, what is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?”
mn12:64.6: ‘As to that, Nāgasamāla, you may remember this discourse on the Dhamma as the Hair-raising Discourse.’
mn12:64.7: That is what the Blessed One said.
mn12:64.8: The venerable Nāgasamāla was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
